precepts.text: Casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you. Go before the Lord and spread the problem out as Hezekiah did.
precepts.point: Rabshakeh had cried in the Jews' language: let not Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord; make an agreement with me by a present and I will carry you to a land like your own; which of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of my hand? The people held their peace at the king's commandment.

note.label: Hope Amid Destruction

precepts.why:
Assyria had already taken the northern kingdom around 722 BC, and around 701 they came for Judah. Their ambassador was talking big: we are going to wipe the floor with you, destroy you and bring you into slavery. Then came a letter of threats. And look at what Hezekiah did with it: he “went up into the house of the Lord, and spread it before the Lord.” He took the letter, spread it out before him, and began to pray: “thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth”.

That is what Peter teaches: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” Sometimes we get in situations and fear comes upon us. Go before the Lord. Whatever the problem is, the Lord knows; go before him and spread it out before him, the way Hezekiah did.

And the Lord answered. Isaiah was not in the room when Hezekiah prayed, but the Lord told him to go to the king and say, “That which thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard.” That is how you know Isaiah was a prophet. Hezekiah cast his care upon the Lord, and that same night one angel smote 185,000 Assyrians.

precepts.text: Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. Idle means idolatrous; the Most High records everything.
precepts.point: Rabshakeh had cried in the Jews' language: let not Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord; make an agreement with me by a present and I will carry you to a land like your own; which of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of my hand? The people held their peace at the king's commandment.

note.label: Hope Amid Destruction

precepts.why:
The Lord asks Sennacherib, “Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? even against the Holy One of Israel.” By his messengers he had reproached the Lord with his boasting words, and every one of them came up into the Lord's ears: “thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears”. The same words also remind our people how we have despised the Lord.

Christ said, “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.” We have to be mindful of this. Sometimes we speak frivolous things and don't realize the Most High is recording everything. Idle means idolatrous: every idolatrous word we speak.

Sennacherib's words were recorded and answered: the Lord put his hook in his nose and turned him back the way he came. So be careful what comes out of your mouth; the Most High hears it all and will bring it to account.

precepts.text: The secrets of wisdom are double to that which is. Christian commentaries put Isaiah 33 entirely in Hezekiah's past so the apologists can say it already happened; the scripture has a double meaning.
precepts.point: Rabshakeh had cried in the Jews' language: let not Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord; make an agreement with me by a present and I will carry you to a land like your own; which of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of my hand? The people held their peace at the king's commandment.

note.label: Hope Amid Destruction

precepts.why:
When you go to the Christian commentaries on Isaiah 33, many of them refer it back to this history: Hezekiah, the king of Assyria, and the angel that wiped them all out. They try to keep every prophecy in the past, as history that already happened. That is why the apologists love to say, that happened already: they read a Christian commentary that said so.

But the scriptures have dual meanings. Job says he “would shew thee the secrets of wisdom, that they are double to that which is!” We all want to know the secrets of wisdom, and they are double to that which is written. You read something, but it has a double meaning behind it. That's how the scriptures are written.

So Isaiah 33:1, “Woe to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled; and dealest treacherously, and they dealt not treacherously with thee!”, was Assyria; but guess who also does that today? The United States of America. To spoil means to rob: the oil of Venezuela, the riches of Libya and of Saddam Hussein, Iran, which did nothing to America. “when thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled”. The history of 2 Kings 19 happened, and the same word speaks to our day.

precepts.text: The fulfillment in Hezekiah's day: the angel of the Lord went out and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand, and Judah woke up to the battle already won; that is how the Lord gets down.
precepts.point: All this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord's. The Most High fights how he wants to fight, not how man thinks it must be done.

note.label: 1 Samuel 17: Not by Sword and Spear

precepts.why:
Here is the fulfillment in Hezekiah's day. The Lord said, “I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake.” And that night “the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.”

Not one sword was lifted by Judah. They went to sleep and woke up to the battle already won. That is how the Lord gets down.

It is the same word David gave before he ever slung the stone: “the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord’s, and he will give you into our hands.”

precepts.text: Judah kept not the commandments, so the Most High rejected the seed of Israel and delivered them into the hand of spoilers.
precepts.point: Because their rage and tumult came up to His ears, the Most High will put His hook in Sennacherib's nose and His bridle in his lips, and turn him back the way he came, which joins with the blast promised in verse 7.

note.label: 2 Kings 19: The Most High Defends Jerusalem

precepts.why:
“Also Judah kept not the commandments of the Lord their God, but walked in the statutes of Israel which they made. And the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, and afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of spoilers.”

That is why Assyria had power to come up at all. The Most High answers Sennacherib, “Hast thou not heard long ago how I have done it, and of ancient times that I have formed it? now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.” He gave Assyria the very ability to lay the cities waste, for his own purpose, because his people kept not his commandments.

But Assyria boasted with the multitude of his chariots, the same as a nation today boasting of its army, military and political system, and lifted his eyes against the Holy One of Israel. So the spoiler is turned back: “I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest.”

precepts.text: Micah, prophesying in the same time, says the Most High will make Samaria a heap, pouring down her stones and laying her idols desolate.
precepts.point: Because their rage and tumult came up to His ears, the Most High will put His hook in Sennacherib's nose and His bridle in his lips, and turn him back the way he came, which joins with the blast promised in verse 7.

note.label: 2 Kings 19: The Most High Defends Jerusalem

precepts.why:
Micah prophesied in the same time: “Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof.” Samaria is made a heap and her idols laid desolate.

That is the work the Most High formed of ancient times and brought to pass through Assyria, “that thou shouldest be to lay waste fenced cities into ruinous heaps.” Samaria fell to Assyria by his hand. Yet when Assyria raged against him and came against Jerusalem, the virgin the daughter of Zion “hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn.” Israel laughs at the enemy, for it is already written that they lose.

precepts.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by the spirit of the Most High, for the battle is His to fight for His people.
precepts.point: Sennacherib departs and dwells at Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smite him with the sword and flee, and Esarhaddon his son reigns in his stead, fulfilling the word of verse 7.

note.label: 2 Kings 19: The Most High Defends Jerusalem

precepts.why:
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.”

Israel did not lift a finger: “the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand.” A score is twenty, so that is a hundred and eighty-five thousand, all dead corpses by morning.

The battle is the Most High’s to fight for his people. This is praying for the death of the enemy and for righteous judgment, and leaving it to his spirit, not to might or power.

precepts.text: Tobit lived in Nineveh in this same time, burying the Israelites Sennacherib slew.
precepts.point: Sennacherib departs and dwells at Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smite him with the sword and flee, and Esarhaddon his son reigns in his stead, fulfilling the word of verse 7.

note.label: 2 Kings 19: The Most High Defends Jerusalem

precepts.why:
Tobit lived in Nineveh in this same time: “if the king Sennacherib had slain any, when he was come, and fled from Judea, I buried them privily; for in his wrath he killed many.”

Sennacherib fled from Judea after the angel of the Lord smote his camp, and returned to dwell at Nineveh, and there in his wrath he slew many Israelites. Tobit buried them in secret. When a Ninevite complained of him to the king, he hid himself for fear of death, “Then all my goods were forcibly taken away, neither was there any thing left me, beside my wife Anna and my son Tobias.”

precepts.text: Tobit records the same murder of Sennacherib by his sons and the reign of Esarhaddon, confirming the history of Kings.
precepts.point: Sennacherib departs and dwells at Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smite him with the sword and flee, and Esarhaddon his son reigns in his stead, fulfilling the word of verse 7.

note.label: 2 Kings 19: The Most High Defends Jerusalem

precepts.why:
“And there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons killed him, and they fled into the mountains of Ararath; and Sarchedonus his son reigned in his stead.”

Tobit records the same murder of Sennacherib by his sons that Kings gives: “Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.” Sarchedonus is Esarhaddon. Two witnesses to one history, and the word of verse 7 fulfilled.

precepts.text: The servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, who spoke the word of the Most High against the blasphemy of the king of Assyria.
precepts.point: Isaiah is a heavy, prophetic book; even the Ethiopian eunuch was reading Isaiah when the spirit sent Philip to help him understand it.

note.label: Isaiah 1: A Sinful Nation, Yet Zion Redeemed With Judgment

precepts.why:
Isaiah saw his vision “in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.” 2 Kings shows him in Hezekiah’s reign: “So the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah. And Isaiah said unto them, Thus shall ye say to your master, Thus saith the Lord, Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.”

Isaiah was a servant and prophet during Hezekiah’s reign, speaking the word of the Most High against the blasphemy of the king of Assyria. This was before the Assyrian captivity destroyed the nation; these are the days in which Isaiah prophesied.

Assyria would put hooks on conquered people and march them out of their land; they were among the most vicious peoples of the ancient world. God said, what you do to people, I am going to do to you.

Then Isaiah sent word: that which thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard. Hezekiah prayed by himself, and Isaiah came and told him God heard your prayer; that is why you need strong men of faith around you.
